new_statements.quote: A phonological word consists of one or more syllables with word stress always occurring on the ultimate syllable. In bisyllabic or trisyllabic words the syllables preceding the stress are voiceless and/or accelerated, accentuating the Chatino trend towards using only monosyllabic words. Tri-syllabic words are very unusual. (p. 248) — Tone is only significant on word-final syllables and thus only the final syllable of a word has tone marked in this work. (p. 9)
new_statements.citation: Pride, Kitty (1965). Chatino syntax. Norman: Summer Institute of Linguistics of the University of Oklahoma. 249 pp.
new_statements.locator: Appendix C 'A note on phonological words', p. 248 (PDF page 250); Introduction §0, p. 9 (PDF page 11) and p. 10 (PDF page 12); §3.7, p. 69 (PDF page 71)
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 rule 01/001/0001.., i.e. fixed final): Pride states word stress is always on the ultimate syllable. It also refines the record by adding that the language is tonal with tone contrastive only on that final stressed syllable, that pretonic syllables are voiceless/accelerated, and that Spanish loans are re-stressed to the final syllable. Describes the Yaitepec dialect, which belongs to Western Highland Chatino (ISO ctp, west2644).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress always falls on the last syllable of the phonological word; the syllables before the stressed final are voiceless and/or accelerated (reduced), so words tend to be monosyllabic and trisyllables are rare. Tone (four registers plus glides) is contrastive only on the word-final, i.e. stressed, syllable. At phrase level the single phrase stress falls on the major word; monosyllabic minor words carry only minor word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None at word level. Phrase level: 'minor words are monosyllabic and occur only in expanded phrases, clauses, or sentences, where they never carry the phrase or sentence stress, but only minor word stress' (p. 10); 'The single phrase stress always occurs on the major word in the expression' (p. 69).
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loanwords of more than one syllable are conformed to the pattern: 'The stress may be shifted to the ultimate syllable and the initial syllables become voiceless, accelerated, or contracted to a consonant cluster' (panela > pnela, semana > smno, machete > wstyi), or the loan is split into a two-word phonological phrase (tienda > tiye ta, culantro > kula ntru) (p. 248). Footnote p. 9 warns that ongoing work on suprasegmentals 'will probably present an alternative solution involving the relationship between stress, tone, and vowel length'; the tone-perturbation system was unsolved at the time.
new_statements.identity_note: Pride 1965 explicitly describes the Yaitepec dialect ('There are at least three distinct and mutually unintelligible dialects with centres in the towns of Yaitepec, Taltaltepec, and Zenzontepec. This work deals with the Yaitepec dialect', p. 9). Santiago Yaitepec Chatino is part of Western Highland Chatino (ISO 639-3 ctp = west2644), so the statement applies to this catalog item. Note that the archive.org Rosetta Project excerpt is filed under the code 'cta' (Tataltepec), which is a mislabel of the archive item, not of the work. The full scan is the University of Florida copy (archive.org id chatinosyntax00prid).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: Rasch 2002:9 quotation confirmed verbatim in the held scanned/PDF (PDF p. 29 = book p. 9); template on pp. 4-6 as described. (2) Deciding source is a 2002 Rice dissertation (grammar-type, 393 pp) whose phonology chapter gives the structural fact (only the final vowel of a phonological word is full and tone-bearing) rather than an explicit stress rule; the StressTyp2 layer rests on a 1965 comparative article we do not hold. sources.quote: Rasch 2002:9: "I understand the distribution of the reduced vowels to be a result of a historical process in which unstressed vowels first gradually harmonized with the following environment. ... in a single phonological word, only one vowel (the final one) is unreduced." Also Rasch 2002:4-5 (Table 3 / Figure 1): the phonological word template (n/nw.)(C(V[reduced]).)CV(7)(n) — every non-final vowel is reduced/unstressed, the final vowel alone is full and tone-bearing.
